rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مأرب is a singular form with three possible vowels on its rāʾ; it is treated as singular in the adjective, a permissible and especially apt agreement at a verse ending.
rows.anchor: ومفردة مأربه مثلثة الراء وعومل في الوصف معاملة مفرده فلم يقل أخر

rows.speaker: الزهر وشيبه
rows.claim: Al-Ahwāzī reports that al-Zuhrī and Shayba read مآرب without a fully articulated hamza, apparently softening it between hamza and vowel.
rows.anchor: عن الزهر وشيبه أنهما قرأ ( مارب ) بغير همز

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: A report transmitted by Aḥmad and others from Wahb describes a forked staff with a hook used to bend or break branches, carry gear, make shade, reach water, and defend the flock.
rows.anchor: روى الامام أحمد وغيره عن وهب في تعين هذه المآرب أنه كان لها شعبتان ومحجم تحتهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabrisī attributes many of the further marvels recounted about the staff to Ibn ʿAbbās; another unnamed account says it could draw water, bear fruit, produce springs, speak, and ward off pests.
rows.anchor: ونقل الطبرسى كثيرا مما ذكر عن ابن عباس رضى الله تعالى عنهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that God prompts Moses to enumerate the staff’s many ordinary benefits before displaying a far greater benefit; the distant demonstrative and vocative signal its importance, while the list and “other uses” magnify its many functions. Naming the staff lets Moses attach these predicates and avoids redundancy.
rows.anchor: أن يعدد المرافق الكثيرة التي علقها بالعصا ويستكثرها ويستعظمها ثم يريه تعالى عقب ذلك الآية العظيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative reads the exchange as Moses presenting the seemingly insignificant dry stick so God can reveal the great power by which He transforms a humble thing; on this reading ما asks for its description or its kind, and تلك belittles it.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون المراد اظهاره عليه السلام حقارتها ليريه عز وجل عظيم ما يخترعه في الخشبة اليابسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposal is that Moses was awed by the signs and the question eased his fear; the repeated address consoles him, and his vague mention of other uses may invite another question and prolong the beloved conversation.
rows.anchor: غلبت عليه الدهشة والهيبة فسأله سبحانه وتكلم معه ازالة لتلك الهيبة والدهشة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Within the awe explanation, the distal demonstrative can portray the staff as far away because Moses is distracted by awe; the unstated further uses might be a bid to hear God speak longer.
rows.anchor: لتنزيل العصا منزلة البعيد لغفلته عليه السلام عنها بما غلب عليه من ذلك

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say God establishes that it is a stick so Moses will not fear when it becomes a snake; al-Ālūsī rejects this proposal, and likewise rejects splitting the exchange into two questions and two answers.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أنه تعالى سأله عليه السلام ليقرره على أنها خشبة حتى إذا قلبها حية لا يخافها وليس بشئ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposals that God first asked what the object was and then what Moses did with it, or separately asked what it was and what he held in his right hand, are weak; the question and answer are each single, as the apparent sense indicates.
rows.anchor: وعلى جميع هذه الأقوال السؤال واحد والجواب واحد كما هو الظاهر وقيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse supports the recommendation of leaning on a staff even for someone who does not need it as a bowstring support.
rows.anchor: استدل بالاية على استحباب التوكؤ على العصا وان لم يكن الشخص بحيث تكون وترا لقوسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse supports economy in grazing: tap branches so leaves fall without stripping them, allowing regrowth for others to use.
rows.anchor: وعلى استحباب الاقتصاد في المرعى بالهش وهو ضرب الشجر ليسقط الورق دون الاستئصال ليخلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After stopping in reverence and returning in great fear, Moses is told to take the serpent; fear is a natural human response to such a sight and does not diminish prophetic rank.
rows.anchor: ولعل ذلك الخوف مما اقتضته الطبيعة البشرية فان البشر بمقتضى طبعه يخاف عند مشاهدة مثل ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the serpent was male.
rows.anchor: وكانت على ما روى عن ابن عباس ذكرا

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb reports that God specified that Moses take the serpent with his right hand.
rows.anchor: وعن وهب أنه تعالى قال له : ( خذها بيمينك )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view explains Moses’ fear as a response to a terrifying event directly from God whose nature he had not yet understood; Abraham did not fear the fire because it came through God’s enemy and its nature was clear.
rows.anchor: إنما خاف عليه السلام لأنه رأى امرا هائلا صدر من الله عز وجل بلا واسطة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says Moses feared because he knew that a member of this species had played a part in Adam’s expulsion from Paradise.
rows.anchor: لأنه عرف ما لقى من ذلك الجنس حيث كان له مدخل في خروج أبيه من الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Coordinating the prohibition with the command signals that not fearing is independently intended, rather than merely instrumental to taking the serpent.
rows.anchor: وإنما عطف النهى على الأمر للاشعار بأن عدم المنهى عنه مقصود لذاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Moses takes it, God will restore the serpent to its former staff-state; that promise explains why Moses should obey and not fear.
rows.anchor: التي هي العصوية استئناف مسوق لتعليل الامتثال بالأمر والنهى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proposed wisdom is that the transformation, command to take it, and prohibition of fear prepare Moses for what will happen with Pharaoh; al-Ālūsī says this may underlie the claim that the promise is a further reassurance and sign, though that reading is not clear.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعضهم أن حكمة انقلابها حية وأمره باخذها ونهيه عن الخوف تانيسه فيما يعلم سبحانه أنه سيقع منه مع فرعون

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Aḥmad and others transmit from Wahb that Moses first covered his hand with his wool garment; an angel asked whether it would protect him if God allowed harm, Moses admitted his weakness, then put his hand in the serpent’s mouth and grasped its jaws; it became his familiar staff again. Al-Ālūsī says the account in which he directly takes it better suits prophetic dignity.
rows.anchor: في رواية الامام أحمد وغيره عن وهب أنه لما امره الله تعالى باخذها ادنى طرف المدرعة على يده

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that Moses was called to take it three times and only took it after the third call; Makkī says the third call included the promise to restore it. Al-Ālūsī finds this remote from prophetic dignity and suggests the report may be unsound.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضى الله تعالى عنهما أنه عليه السلام نودى المرة الأولى يا موسى خذها فلم ياخذها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sīra derives from travel and first meant the form or state of a journey, then broadened to a general manner or state; it can mean a way or school, as in the cited line about a manner one has followed.
rows.anchor: والسيرة فعلة من السير تقال للهيءة والحالة الواقعة فيه ثم جردت لمطلق الهيئة والحالة

rows.speaker: الحوفى
rows.claim: Al-Ḥawfī’s analysis treats سِيرَتَهَا as a second object with a preposition omitted, originally إلى سيرتها or لسيرتها; Ibn Mālik adopts this analysis and Ibn Hishām approves it.
rows.anchor: مفعول ثان لسنعيدها على حذف الجار نحو

rows.speaker: الزمخشرى
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī allows اعاد from عاده, meaning “return to it,” to govern two objects directly; the cited line by Zuhayr uses عادك to mean “turned you away.”
rows.anchor: بمعنى عاد اليه ومنه قول زهير

rows.speaker: الأصمعى
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī and other lexicographers attest that عاد can take a direct object with the sense of turning or returning, supporting the transitive analysis.
rows.anchor: نقل الطيبى عن الاصمعى أن عادك في البيت متعد بمعنى صرفك

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ analyzes سِيرَتَهَا as an appositive of inclusion replacing the object pronoun in سنعيدها.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء : هي بدل من ضمير المفعول بدل اشتمال

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects treating سِيرَتَهَا as an adverbial accusative because a specific manner is not an indefinite adverbial; a preposition في is needed, and omission is only poetic or anomalous.
rows.anchor: وتعقبه أبو حيان قائلا : أن سيرتها وطريقتها ظرف مختص فلا يتعدى اليه الفعل

rows.speaker: نحاة المغرب
rows.claim: Grammarians of the Maghrib classify derived nouns such as مذهب as an indefinite type of adverbial, without distinguishing those ending in tāʾ; on their analysis this accusative is neither anomalous nor forced.
rows.anchor: وفي شرح التسهيل عن نحاة المغرب انهم قسموا المبهم إلى أقسام منها المشتق من الفعل

rows.speaker: الزمخشرى
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī prefers parsing سنعيدها as complete on its own and سِيرَتَهَا as an absolute object of an understood verb: “we will restore it, moving in its former manner,” as when Moses leaned on it and used it for his flock.
rows.anchor: وجوز الزمخشرى واستحسنه أن يكون ( سنعيدها ) مستقلا بنفسه غير متعلق بسيرتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the Zamakhsharī parsing is good in meaning, with the implied participial clause either circumstantial or a new sentence, but it departs from the immediately apparent construction.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه جعل الجملة من الفعل المقدر وفاعله حالا ويجوز أن يكون استئنافا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse indicates that a thing may change its reality, as when a staff becomes a serpent; divine creative command can bring this about.
rows.anchor: والآية ظاهرة في جواز انقلاب الشئ عن حقيقته كانقلاب النحاس إلى الذهب وبه قال جمع

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some deny that a reality can turn into another, calling alteration of essences impossible and therefore outside the scope of divine power; al-Ālūsī rejects this denial.
rows.anchor: وقيل : لا يجوز لأن قلب الحقائق محال والقدرة لا تتعلق به

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: One account of transformation is that God creates gold in place of the copper; another, held by some theologians who regard atoms as alike in accepting attributes, removes copper’s property and creates gold’s property. The author favors the latter; only being copper and gold at once is impossible.
rows.anchor: يخلق بدل النحاس مثلا ذهبا على ماهو رأى بعض المحققين أو بأن يسلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request for ease is tied to the command to go to Pharaoh (20:24): Moses recognizes the immense mission and asks God to make him patient under its trials and to ease it by enabling its means and removing obstacles; the prayer expresses utter dependence on God.
rows.anchor: أنه عليه السلام علم من الأمر بالذهاب اليه والتعليل بالعلة المذكورة أنه كلف امرا عظيما

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some connect the request to all of God’s address from “I am your Lord” through this point: Moses seeks an expanded heart to grasp subtle knowledge and revelation, perform worship fully, and endure preaching’s hardships.
rows.anchor: أن هذا القول معلق بما خاطبه الله تعالى به من لدن قوله سبحانه ( انى انا ربك فاخلع نعليك )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says Moses faced difficult duties in receiving revelation, serving God, and ordering the lower world; he sought enough strength to manage both worlds, since attending to one can impede the other.
rows.anchor: احتاج إلى تكاليف شاقة من تلقى الوحى والمواظبة على خدمة الخالق سبحانه وتعالى واصلاح العالم السفلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī also reads the command to Pharaoh as implying prophetic duties toward God and people; Moses senses all of them and asks for help to fulfill them perfectly, so the request need not be restricted to the earliest divine address.
rows.anchor: أن الأمر بالذهاب إلى فرعون قد انطوى فيه الاشارة إلى منصب الرسالة المستتبع تكاليف لائقة به

rows.speaker: علماء الرسوم
rows.claim: For the formal scholars, “chest” here means the heart, either because it perceives or because it is the means of perception.
rows.anchor: أن الصدر عنه علماء الرسوم يراد منه القلب لأنه المدرك أو مما به الادراك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added لِي intensifies the request: first the object of opening or easing is left implicit, then صدرى and أمري specify it; without لِي the clause would be complete but less elaborated. The same applies to both requests.
rows.anchor: وفي ذكر كلمة ( لى ) مع انتظام الكلام بدونها تاكيد لطلب الشرح والتيسير بابهام المشروح والميسر اولا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say لِي adds a stronger connection, as in “The reckoning of people has drawn near” (21:1); al-Ālūsī replies that this does not conflict with the preceding explanation.
rows.anchor: وقيل : ذكر ( لى ) لزيادة الربط كما في قوله تعالى ( اقترب للناس حسابهم )

rows.speaker: الانتصاف
rows.claim: Al-Intiṣāf says لِي shows that the benefit of opening the chest returns to Moses, since God is unaffected by whether it exists; al-Ālūsī applies the same point to the request to ease his task.
rows.anchor: وفي الانتصاف أن فائدة ذكرها الدلالة على أن منفعة شرح الصدر راجعة اليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to go with Aaron is a new sentence explaining what God’s special favor to Moses entails.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى ( اذهب انت واخوتك باياتى ( استئناف مسوق لبيان ما هو المقصود بالاصطناع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parsing makes أخوك the subject of an understood “let your brother go,” in keeping with Moses’ request; another coordinates it with the implicit subject pronoun in اذهب, although a construction valid only as a dependent may not stand independently.
rows.anchor: أي وليذهب اخوك حسبما استدعيت وقيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs are identified variously as the hand, staff, and speech knot; Ibn ʿAbbās says the nine signs, while another view says only the first two, with the plural commonly used for a pair.
rows.anchor: والايات المعجزات والمراد بها في قول اليد والعصا وحل العقدة وعن ابن عباس الآيات التسع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The view that the signs are the staff and hand is supported by Pharaoh’s request for a sign and Moses’ presentation of these two, which he calls “two proofs” (28:32).
rows.anchor: قال له عليه السلام : فات با اية القى العصا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some explain the plural even for two miracles because each contains several signs: the staff’s transformation, size, speed, submission, safety in its mouth, and return, and the hand’s whiteness, radiance, and restoration.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : أنهما وان كانتا اثنتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A broader view takes the signs as all Moses’ miracles and revelation, but al-Ālūsī favors the staff and hand: these alone are named as signs immediately before the command to go, and other signs such as resolving the speech knot are not called signs there (20:22).
rows.anchor: واذي يميل اليه القلب أنه العصا واليد لما سمعت من المؤيد مع ما تقدم من أنه تعالى بعد ما أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The باء marks accompaniment, not transmission: Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh equipped with and relying on the signs to fulfill the mission; this implies the signs were already present, while most of the nine had not yet occurred.
rows.anchor: ثم أن الباء للمصاحبة لا للتعدية إذ المراد ذهابهما إلى فرعون ملتبسين بالايات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb is from الوَنَى, “slackness,” and is normally intransitive; when made transitive it takes في or عن. Some Baghdadi grammarians instead treat it as a defective verb meaning زال, “continue,” an analysis Ibn Mālik chose; the lexicon explains لا يني يفعل as “keeps doing.”
rows.anchor: من الونى بمعنى الفتور وهوفعل لازم وإذا عدى عدى بفى وبعن

rows.speaker: ابن وثاب
rows.claim: Ibn Waththāb reads the tāʾ with kasra by vowel assimilation to the following nūn; ʿAbd Allāh’s codex has لاتهنا, with the same sense of not flagging.
rows.anchor: وقرا ابن وثاب ( ولاتنيا ) بكسر التاء اتباعه لحركة النون وفي مصحف عبد الله ( لاتهنا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of “in My remembrance” is to remember God through the noble attributes and good acts befitting Him while conveying His message and calling people to worship.
rows.anchor: بما يليق بى من الصفات الجليلة والأفعال الجميلة عند تبليغ رسالتى والدعاء إلى عبادتى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A view transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās reads the command as “do not slack in conveying My message,” since remembrance can stand metaphorically for all worship and is its greatest form.
rows.anchor: وروى ذلك عن ابن عباس رضى الله تعالى عنهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view means: do not forget God wherever you go; seek His help and support, knowing that nothing can be accomplished without remembering Him.
rows.anchor: لا تنسيانى حيثما تقلبتما واستمدا به العون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron is included in the dual prohibition even if he was absent at that moment, by the grammatical practice of giving precedence to the present addressee; this poses no difficulty.
rows.anchor: وجمع هرون مع موسى عليه السلام في صيغة نهى الحاضر بناء على القول بغيبته إذ ذاك للتغلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here منها refers to the earth.
rows.anchor: ( منها ( أي من الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity was created from earth through the creation of Adam: every person shares in Adam’s creation because his distinctive formation contained the prototype for the whole species and its effects.
rows.anchor: في ضمن خلق ابيكم ادم عليه السلام منها فان كل فرد من افراد البشر له حظ من خلقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that human bodies come from semen produced by foods, which in turn derive from the earth through intermediate stages.
rows.anchor: المعنى خلقنا ابدانكم من النطفة المتولدة من الاغذية

rows.speaker: عطاء الخرسانى
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī reports that an angel takes soil from the place where a person will be buried and sprinkles it on the semen, so the person is created from both soil and semen.
rows.anchor: عن عطاء الخرسانى قال : أن الملك ينطلق فياخذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Return to the earth means death and the dispersal of bodily parts; this and the following account describe what generally happens, since some bodies, including prophets’ bodies, do not decay.
rows.anchor: بالاماتة وتفريق الأجزاء وهذا وكذا ما بعد مبنى على الغالب بناء على أن من الناس من لا يبلى جسده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition “in” rather than “to” emphasizes the long-lasting residence of people in the earth.
rows.anchor: وايثار كلمة فى على كلمة إلى للدلالة على الأستقرار المديد فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The resurrection reassembles the scattered bodily parts mixed with earth into their former form and returns souls to them from their resting place.
rows.anchor: بتاليف اجزائكم المتفتته المختلطة بالتراب على الهيئة السابقة ورد الأرواح من مقرها اليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The resurrection is “another time” because the first creation from earth was also an emergence from it, although not in the same manner; tāra originally denotes a single course or occurrence and then each renewed act, like marra.
rows.anchor: وكون هذا الأخراج تاره أخرى باعتبار أن خلقهم من الأرض أخراج لهم منها وان لم يكن على نهج التاره الثانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Placing human creation and resurrection after the plants’ emergence from earth draws a parallel: both are delicate bodies brought forth from dense soil.
rows.anchor: فقد تضمن كل أخراج اجسام لطيفة من الترباء الكثيفة وخروج الاموات اشبه شئ بخروج النبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In an esoteric reading, Ṭāhā can address the Prophet as purified through God and guiding to Him, or as one who circumambulates the Kaʿba of oneness in the sanctuary of identity and guides pure souls to lofty stations.
rows.anchor: ( طه ) يا طاهرا بنا هاديا الينا أو يا طائف كعبة الاحدية في حرم الهوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An abjad reading assigns Ṭāʾ the value nine, whose cumulative numbers total 45, the value of Adam; Hāʾ is five, whose cumulative numbers total 15, the value of Ḥawwāʾ. Together they signify that Muhammad is the father and mother of creation.
rows.anchor: أن ط لكونها بحساب الجمل تسعة وإذا جمع ما انطوت

rows.speaker: ابن الفارض
rows.claim: Ibn al-Fāriḍ’s verse, spoken in the voice of the Muhammadan reality, says that although it is Adam’s son in outward form, its inner meaning bears witness to its fatherhood.
rows.anchor: قد اشار إلى ذلك عارف بن الفارض قدس سره بقوله على لسان الحقيقة المحمدية

rows.speaker: عبد الغنى النابلسى
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Ghanī al-Nābulusī’s verse says that all creatures formed from the Prophet’s light, echoing the esoteric claim that he is the source-parent of creation.
rows.anchor: الشيخ عبد الغنى النابلسى عليه الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another abjad interpretation totals Ṭāhā as fourteen, signaling the full-moon state and addressing the Prophet as the moon of the world of contingent existence.
rows.anchor: الحساب اربعة عشر وهو إشارة إلى مرتبة البدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One esoteric reading says the reminder recalls the days of union before souls entered bodies and promises their return; alternatively, it reminds them of those days to stir longing, tears, and effort toward regaining them.
rows.anchor: أي إلا لتذكر من يخشى ايام الوصال التى كانت قبل تعلق الأرواح بالابدان وتخبرهم بانها يحصل نحوها لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some identify those who fear as scholars, citing 35:28; since knowledge can invite vanity and pride, the reminder of God’s greatness protects scholars from these faults.
rows.anchor: من يخشى هم العلماء لقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account describes the Throne as a great created body of radiant light and the locus where the simple light of intellect shines; its honor comes from the incomprehensible divine istiwāʾ. Another says it consists of four differently colored lights named by the four glorifications; the contemporary Kashfiyya sect adopted this view and called it al-Aṭlas.
rows.anchor: العرش جسم عظيم خلقه الله تعالى كما قيل من نور شعشعانى وجعله موضع نور العقل البسيط

rows.speaker: بعض الصوفية
rows.claim: Some Sufis take the Throne as a symbol of the believer’s heart, whose relation to the well-known Throne is as a mustard seed to a plain or a drop to the sea; it is the place of divine regard, manifestation, command, and descent.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعض الصوفية أن العرش إشارة إلى قلب المؤمن الذى نسبة العرش المشهور اليه كنسبة الخردلة إلى الفلاة

rows.speaker: الغزالى
rows.claim: Al-Ghazālī cites the saying that neither heaven nor earth encompasses God but the gentle, tranquil heart of His believing servant; al-Qūnawī transmits a variant describing the heart as pious and pure.
rows.anchor: وفي احياء العلوم بحجة الأسلام الغزالى قال الله تعالى لم يسعنى سمائى ولا ارضى ووسعنى قلب عبدى المؤمن

rows.speaker: صدر الدين القونوى
rows.claim: The heart that can manifest the divine is not the pineal organ, which is too lowly in form; it is the comprehensive human reality joining divine qualities with spiritual and natural cosmic traits, while the pineal organ is the dwelling-place of the outward heart-image.
rows.anchor: وليس هذا القلب عبارة عن البضعة الصنوبرية فانها عند كل عاقل احقر من حيث الصورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heart’s “encompassing” of God means it is a comprehensive manifestation of the divine names and attributes, without implying indwelling, union, division, or the eternal subsisting in the contingent.
rows.anchor: كونه مظهرا جامعا للاسماء والصفات على وجه لا ينافى تنزيه الحق سبحانه من الحلول والاتحاد

rows.speaker: العراقى
rows.claim: Although the saying is widespread among Sufis, al-ʿIrāqī says he found no source for it.
rows.anchor: العراقى : لم ار له أصلا

rows.speaker: ابن تيمية
rows.claim: Ibn Taymiyya calls the saying an Israelite report and says it has no known chain from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: شيخ الاسلام ابن تيمية : هو مذكور في الاسرائيليات

rows.speaker: وهب ابن منبه
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī suggests the saying may allude to Aḥmad’s al-Zuhd report from Wahb ibn Munabbih: God opens the heavens for Ezekiel to see the Throne, then says heaven and earth cannot contain Him, but the gentle heart of His believing servant can.
rows.anchor: عن وهب ابن منبه قال : أن الله تعالى فتح السموات
